pr_title: If a ticket key callback returns 0 in TLSv1.3 don't send a ticket (3.0 backport)
pr_body:
If we can't construct the ticket don't send one. This requires a change
to the TLS state machine to be able to a handle a construction function
deciding not to send a message after all.

Fixes #18977

This is a backport of #18990 to the 3.0 branch. It does not include the commit from that PR which introduces a new enum because that change is probably too invasive for 3.0.
pr_comments: This pull request is ready to merge

issue_context.title: OpenSSL doesn't properly encode NewSessionTicket when using SSL_CTX_set_tlsext_ticket_key_cb callback that returns 0
comments: Thanks for the reproducer. I can replicate this in master too.

The problem is that we are issuing a TLSv1.2 format ticket in this case.

In TLSv1.2 if the callback returns 0, then we just issue a 0 length ticket. However, a further problem is that TLSv1.3 does not allow 0 length tickets (must be at least 1 byte), so its actually unclear what the correct behaviour should be in this case.

We use `SSL_CONNECTION_IS_TLS13` elsewhere. Can we check for that and append 4 bytes for ticket_lifetime, 4 bytes for ticket_age_add, no bytes for `ticket_nonce`, which I believe you can omit if it's empty (edit: eh, this is probably wrong), and 1 byte for the length of the `ticket`, with value 0?

It's actually quite unclear what a zero length ticket even means in TLSv1.2. But at least it is syntactically allowed.

For TLSv1.3 sending a 1 byte ticket would be possible - but this would make it indistinguishable from a real ticket to the client - so the client would be behaving reasonably if it cached that ticket and then attempted to use it (possibly repeatedly) for resumption attempts. This is probably not the behaviour we want.

RFC 8446 (TLSv1.3) does say this about the `ticket_lifetime` field:

>    ticket_lifetime:  Indicates the lifetime in seconds as a 32-bit
      unsigned integer in network byte order from the time of ticket
      issuance.  Servers MUST NOT use any value greater than
      604800 seconds (7 days).  The value of zero indicates that the
      ticket should be discarded immediately.  Clients MUST NOT cache
      tickets for longer than 7 days, regardless of the ticket_lifetime,
      and MAY delete tickets earlier based on local policy.  A server
      MAY treat a ticket as valid for a shorter period of time than what
      is stated in the ticket_lifetime.

So, potentially, we could send a 1 byte ticket with a ticket_lifetime of 0 indicating that the ticket should be discarded immediately.  This is only a "should" though, so some clients could potentially cache it anyway.
Can we also not send a `NewSessionTicket` message if the callback failed to produce the required material?

> Can we also not send a NewSessionTicket message if the callback failed to produce the required material?

At the point the callback is called we have already decided to send a NewSessionsTicket and have already constructed the message header (higher up in the callstack). The OpenSSL state machine doesn't currently have a mechanism for aborting the construction of the current message, rolling back and deciding not to send it after all. You can only abort the whole handshake or succeed. So that route seems quite hard (although possible).

I have a fix for master in #18990. It's a bit too invasive for backport to 3.0/1.1.1 but I think I can create a less invasive version that is more suitable there - but I'll wait for review of #18990 first.

> It's actually quite unclear what a zero length ticket even means in TLSv1.2. But at least it is syntactically allowed.

I think it's pretty clear, actually:

```quote
3.3.  NewSessionTicket Handshake Message

   [...]  If the server determines that it does not want to include a
   ticket after it has included the SessionTicket extension in the
   ServerHello, then it sends a zero-length ticket in the
   NewSessionTicket handshake message.
```

> For TLSv1.3 sending a 1 byte ticket would be possible - but this would make it indistinguishable from a real ticket to the client - so the client would be behaving reasonably if it cached that ticket and then attempted to use it (possibly repeatedly) for resumption attempts. This is probably not the behaviour we want.

We would of course reject such a 1-byte ticket when it came back to us, falling back to a full handshake.
Which is ... maybe not so bad, given how invasive #18990 is.

> I think it's pretty clear, actually:

Great - thanks. Somehow I couldn't find that reference.

> maybe not so bad, given how invasive https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/18990 is.

I'm fairly sure I can create a version of #18990 that is a lot less invasive (basically don't introduce the enum but keep it as a normal int). That seems like it might make it more suitable for a backport, i.e. do #18990 as-is for master, but a less invasive version for 3.0/1.1.1

> We would of course reject such a 1-byte ticket when it came back to us, falling back to a full handshake.
Which is ... maybe not so bad, given how invasive https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/18990 is.

:vomiting_face:
Reopening this. It was auto-closed due to the merge of #18990. However that PR only addresses master and we still need a backport to 3.0.
The fix was backported to 3.0 by #19249 which has now been merged. Closing this.

> The fix was backported to 3.0 by #19249 which has now been merged. Closing this.

Am I out of luck if I'm working with 1.1.1?
Unfortunately 1.1.1 is in security-fix only mode so the fix won't be backported there.
Cool, extra motivation to move on to newer versions. Thanks for the fix!

review_comments: So likewise here, ...  Pausing review here, until the enum, macro, literal ints issue is resolved.

Could we at least have internal macros for these constants (2, ...)?
Is `statem.h` a public header?  If not, introduction of a purely internal enum does not introduce any API issues I can think of.  You can still use the same enum from master I think, but otherwise equivalent internal macros.

Even if we do not change the return value signatures, this would still touch a lot of code and is essentially a refactoring, i.e. everywhere we have a "return" statement in any construction function would have to change to use the macros. I do not think that kind of change is appropriate for 3.0 (i.e. it does not meet the requirements of the [stable release updates policy](https://www.openssl.org/policies/technical/stable-release-updates.html))

That's a tenable position, but one might also note that making all those point changes could make it easier to backport future PRs that overlap the code in question.  Your call I guess.  If you still think this is the best way forward, I'll continue the review as-is...
It's a tricky call (both ways have good arguments), but I'd still call it on the side of changing less code in the 3.0 branch - so I still think the way in this PR is the best way forward.
